mormon.title: Sharing Jesus with a Latter-day Saint friend
mormon.intro: Not to win an argument. To help a real person meet the real Jesus, with gentleness (2 Timothy 2:24–25). Built from documented ex-Mormon conversions and from ministries with decades in this work.
mormon.html:
Say this early, long before any crisis
You, over hot chocolate

"If the church ever turned out not to be true, that would not mean Jesus is not real."

Say it while everything is calm, so a friend has somewhere to land later. A faith crisis without it usually ends in atheism, not in Christ.

What brings Latter-day Saints to Christ, ranked by their own stories
1

Reading the New Testament for itself

The most common starting point. A missionary in Orlando set out to convert a Baptist pastor. The pastor fed him, gave him the gospel, and asked him to "read the Bible as a child would read it." Eighteen months later he gave his life to Christ, knowing the cost. His mother, a tenured BYU professor, read it again and "saw the difference between their Mormon Christ and the biblical Jesus." She resigned on 3/16, in honor of John 3:16 (Lynn Wilder, Unveiling Grace).

2

Grace, after years of trying to be worthy

The cycle of worthiness interviews produces a documented fatigue. What lands is full forgiveness that does not depend on how the week went.

3

Facts crack the shelf, and a friend decides where they land

The CES Letter gets people out of the church. It does not get them to Jesus. When a faith is all true or all false, the usual landing is atheism. Every story has two parts. Evidence broke the shelf. Then one Christian, loving them without conditions, carried them to Jesus instead of nowhere.

4

Being loved with no agenda

Their culture has a word for friendship with a goal attached: friendshipping. A friendship that survives their doubts, and their leaving, is startling. The version they grew up with is conditional.

The method

Witness to Christ, not against Mormonism

Speak about Jesus as the one who took your place, not just a good example. See your friend as burdened, not an opponent.

Ask questions instead of making statements

Two questions do most of the work. "What exactly do you mean by that word?" makes them define it. "How did you come to that conclusion?" moves the burden back. Both beat a testimony played as a trump card.

Learn their vocabulary first

Grace, salvation, eternal life, atonement. You share the words, not the meanings. Define them before you argue, or you will agree loudly while meaning opposite things.

Use only their own sources

The Gospel Topics Essays, the Joseph Smith Papers, church manuals. Never use a claim you cannot document from an LDS source. One overstated attack discredits ten true ones and feeds the persecution story.

Never mock the temple or the garments

The fastest way to end the friendship for good. In 2003, street preachers at Temple Square desecrated garments in public. Twenty-three evangelical ministers denounced them. It backfires twice: their doctrine reads opposition as proof the church is true, so every yelled slogan works like a testimony meeting.

Never use the weak arguments

This site marks the claims that do not hold up. Repeating one hands your friend an easy win and discredits your true ones.

Never expect a decision today

Exits take months or years. Plant one thing per conversation and let it sit. If your friendship depends on agreement, you offer the same deal the church does.

Pray, and keep praying

You cannot argue anyone into the kingdom. "No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him" (John 6:44).

How it actually goes

Exits take years. Almost every one has a Christian in it who stayed.

When they say prophets were only imperfect men

The standard answer when Joseph Smith's conduct comes up. The church openly denies that prophets are perfect, so Joseph sinned bounces off. Two things do not bounce.

  1. Their own words about the man. D&C 135:3 says Joseph "has done more, save Jesus only, for the salvation of men in this world, than any other man." The church set that standard, not you. The hymn Praise to the Man is still sung to him.
  2. Sinning is not the same as lying about revelation. A prophet may lose his temper. He may not lie about what God told him. Every book and ordinance runs through his honesty. The record is hard here. Public denials of polygamy, while he was secretly married to more than thirty women. A revelation threatening Emma by name. Revelations edited after the fact. The Book of Abraham. Ask him: "I am not asking whether Joseph was perfect. I am asking whether he told the truth about the revelations. Which of those does Deuteronomy 18 speak to?"

The fruits test in Matthew 7:15–20 is fair game too. Missionaries use it for Joseph. Accept it, then open the Admitted column of this site and weigh the fruit.

Argue from their canon, not from yours

Article of Faith 8 trusts the Bible only "as far as it is translated correctly." That makes it the least trusted book they own. The Book of Mormon is "the most correct of any book on earth." Your friend can wave off Isaiah. They cannot wave off Moroni.

  1. One God, or many gods. Alma 11:28–29 asks if there is more than one God, and answers no.
  2. A God who changes. Moroni 8:18 calls God "unchangeable from all eternity to all eternity." The King Follett sermon says God was once as we are now.
  3. Polygamy. Jacob 2:24 calls the many wives of David and Solomon abominable. D&C 132 calls them a gift from God.
  4. A second chance. Alma 34:32–35 says "this life is the time to prepare to meet God." A whole temple system is built on saving the dead.

Then ask the question that lands: "If I showed you that the Book of Mormon disagrees with what your church teaches today, which one would you go with?"

When the missionaries are at your table

Open the door. They are eighteen to twenty, homesick, living on very little. Feed them. You may be the only committed Christian who ever shares a meal with them, and more than one famous exit began that way. Here is your best move for each of the five lessons in Preach My Gospel.

  1. The Restoration. Total apostasy after the apostles, then restoration through Joseph Smith. Then pray for a feeling about the Book of Mormon. Ask: "Jesus said the gates of hell would not prevail against his church. If it failed for seventeen hundred years, was he wrong?" On the feeling, offer to test it against Scripture instead (Matthew 16:18; Acts 17:11; Galatians 1:8).
  2. The Plan of Salvation. Spirits before birth, three degrees of glory, a kingdom for nearly everyone. Ask: "Scripture says we become the children of God by adoption. Does that not mean we were not his children before?" Then: "If almost everyone gets a kingdom, what did Jesus save us from?" (Romans 8:15; John 1:12).
  3. The gospel. Faith, repentance, baptism by their authority, enduring to the end, and grace after all we can do. The most fruitful question in this work: "What must I do to be completely forgiven, and have you done it?"
  4. The commandments. Follow the prophet, the Word of Wisdom, tithing, chastity. Do not fight the rules. Probe what they do: "When you keep all of it, does it ever feel like enough? How would you know?" Then say that for you, obedience is thanks for a salvation you already have.
  5. Laws and ordinances. Priesthood, temple ordinances, eternal marriage, baptism for the dead. Open Hebrews together (10:11–14; 7:23–25) and ask why Jesus is seated. Because the work is finished.

Four things to know about how it goes

  1. When they bear testimony. I know the church is true is a trained move. Do not argue with the feeling. Question the test: "How do you tell a feeling that is from God apart from one that is only deeply felt?" People of many faiths report the same burning confirmation of opposite things. God gave a test for prophets that does not run on feelings (Deuteronomy 18:22; 1 John 4:1). Moroni 10:4 asks you to pray about the book, but it assumes the answer. 1 Corinthians 15:3–8 rests on witnesses instead. Jeremiah 17:9 and Proverbs 14:12 say why the heart alone is no safe judge. Then say: "My confidence holds up on my worst-feeling day. It is not in my feelings about Jesus. It is in what he did in history. My feelings have bad days. The empty tomb does not."
  2. The shelf. Members shelve the doubts they cannot resolve, until the shelf breaks. You cannot see the shelf, so do not demand an answer. Say: "You do not have to answer that now. Just sit with it."
  3. Milk before meat. Your friend may honestly not know the hard history, and the missionaries at your table may know less than you do. Never say the church is hiding it. Say: "I read this in an LDS source. Can you help me understand it?"
  4. Count the cost out loud. Doubting can mean bishop interviews, a warned spouse, weddings they are not invited to, distance from family. The family cost is enormous. Never gloat over a crack in their faith. Say: "I know what this could cost you. I am not going anywhere either way." Be the unconditional community the ward cannot be. Expect years.

The gospel side by side, and the bridge across

  1. God. An exalted man, one of many gods, once as we are now. Or God "from everlasting to everlasting," with none formed before or after him (Psalm 90:2; Isaiah 43:10).
  2. Jesus. Firstborn spirit child, our elder brother, who reached godhood. Or the eternal Word who was God, made flesh, maker of all things (John 1:1, 14; Colossians 1:16).
  3. Worthiness becomes grace. Resurrection for all, then exaltation by ordinances, covenants and worthiness, after all we can do. Or a gift by faith, "not of works, lest any man should boast" (2 Nephi 25:23; Ephesians 2:8–9; John 19:30). Say: "I am not worthy either. That is exactly who Jesus came for." In Romans 4:5, God justifies the ungodly.
  4. Exaltation becomes adoption. Becoming a god one day, or a child of God today. Romans 8:15–17 gives an inheritance received, not a rank achieved. Adoption quietly undoes the pre-existence story.
  5. The endless temple becomes the finished cross. Hebrews 10:11–14. Their priests stand daily. Our high priest sat down. Ask why he is sitting.
  6. Enduring becomes assurance. A recommend renewed, worthiness reviewed by interview. Or "he that believeth on the Son hath everlasting life," present tense, no condemnation (John 3:36; Romans 8:1). 1 John 5:13 says "that ye may know that ye have eternal life." Ask if they know.
  7. Forsaking becomes coming home. The standard set by Kimball is crushing. In Luke 15 the father runs to his son mid-confession (1 John 1:9). Listen for their tiredness.
  8. Destiny. Members become gods with eternal increase (D&C 132:19–20). Or adopted children glorified with Christ, worshippers for ever, never rival gods (Romans 8:17; Revelation 22:3).
  9. The Great Apostasy becomes the Christ who held. Ask: "Which is more likely? That Jesus lost his church for seventeen hundred years, or that he kept his promise?" (Matthew 16:18; Ephesians 3:21).
